newsitem.title: USA: SEC considers way to expand US press access abroad.
newsitem.headline: SEC considers way to expand US press access abroad.

text.p: The Securities and Exchange Commission on Wednesday offered for public comment a proposal that would expand U.S. journalists' access to company press conferences abroad.

The issue revolves around the occasional exclusion of U.S. journalists from press conferences regarding securities offerings and tender offers. In such cases, the U.S. journalists may receive information on the offerings with a delay of an hour or more.

SEC officials said the decision to exclude the American press was based on some companies' fears that if they spoke to U.S. journalists, they would become subject to the full array of American securities laws.

The SEC's proposed rules are aimed at clarifying the conditions under which journalists would be permitted access to offshore press conferences, press meetings and to the release of press-related materials.

At a meeting, SEC Chairman Arthur Levitt said that the proposal recognizes that given modern communications, information released to the press anywhere will reach the United States "almost instantaneously."

"To apply the full measure of U.S. securities laws to such companies serves no logical purpose," Levitt said. "Though the aim is to protect investors, this practice effectively curtails the amount of information available to them."
He added, "We will not only liberalize these rules, but we will include safeguards to protect investors against abuse."

One commissioner, Steven Wallman, said he was sympathetic to the broad issue but took issue with parts of the proposal, such as a process for releasing materials that he said might be overly costly to companies. He said he was hopeful that those issues could be addressed during the comment period.
